routes.description: Establish that a first-century Jewish preacher existed behind the Christian traditions by combining early Pauline testimony, multiple source traditions, historically plausible context, and the distinction between legendary development and personal nonexistence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if independent and comparatively early evidence is more probable given an earthly Jesus than a wholly mythical origin, while source criticism can reject legendary details without eliminating the underlying person.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative source pattern makes a historical Jewish person behind the traditions more probable than an origin without such a person.

centralBridges.description: Establish that early Pauline material refers to an earthly Jewish Jesus and connects Paul with people represented as Jesus's brother and disciple.
Establish that multiple comparatively early traditions provide historically significant attestation rather than merely repeating one late narrative.
Explain why proclamation of a crucified Messiah is more expected as a response to an actual execution than as an invention from prevailing Jewish expectations.
Show that mythic, miraculous, or scripturally patterned accretions can surround a person whose existence remains historically recoverable.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Prefer explanations grounded in first-century Jewish and Roman conditions over proposed analogies whose relevant evidence is culturally remote or later.
Apply comparative historical probability through source proximity, independence, contextual fit, and explanatory economy.

routes.description: Establish that Christianity can be explained without a recoverable first-century preacher by challenging the independence, authenticity, and terrestrial meaning of the sources while offering celestial, scriptural, and literary pathways for the development of Jesus traditions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if purported historical anchors remain dependent, ambiguous, interpolated, or methodologically circular and the emergence of the exalted Christ is at least as well explained by mythic and scriptural development as by an ordinary founder.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving evidence does not require a historical preacher and remains compatible with Christianity developing without such a person.

centralBridges.description: Interpret the earliest Pauline Christ as accessible through revelation and scripture and as compatible with a celestial death followed by later historicization.
Show that Gospel sources, oral traditions, and external notices do not constitute securely independent attestations of an underlying person.
Provide a plausible pathway from Jewish divine, scriptural, or mythic materials to terrestrial narratives about Jesus.
Show that positing an ordinary teacher does not by itself explain the emergence and character of the exalted miracle-working Christ.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve material uncertainty about historicizing passages through interpolation arguments, manuscript gaps, and disputed authorship.
Challenge historical reconstructions whose chronology, narrative anchors, or organizing paradigms presuppose the person they are meant to establish.

sections.title: Historical Method and Comparative Burden
sections.rationale: Defines the probability standard for the motion and tests how source proximity, independence, background knowledge, and competing explanatory paradigms bear on existence.

sections.title: Pauline Jesus and Textual Foundations
sections.rationale: Addresses the earliest principal evidence, including earthly or celestial reference, biographical silence, revelation, associates, interpolation, authorship, and textual authenticity.

sections.title: Gospel Traditions and Historical Recovery
sections.rationale: Tests whether multiple Gospel traditions preserve recoverable information about a person or instead reflect dependent literary, scriptural, and legendary construction.

sections.title: External Attestation and Chronology
sections.rationale: Examines whether non-Christian notices, ancient critics, oral transmission, and proposed early sources independently anchor Jesus or merely attest later Christian claims.

sections.title: Movement Origins, Jewish Context, and the Crucified Messiah
sections.rationale: Compares an executed Jewish founder followed by resurrection belief with celestial, theophanic, or scriptural origin models and asks which better explains the movement's emergence.

sections.title: Legendary Development and Explanatory Fit
sections.rationale: Determines whether mythic accretions are compatible with an underlying person and whether a minimal historical figure or a mythic origin better accounts for the resulting Christ traditions.
